extracted.intended_audience: novelists and creative writers interested in using or studying the epistolary form
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for novelists on composing fiction using letters, diary entries, emails, or other personal correspondence forms; covers form choices, voice, viewpoint, dramatic structure, and practical techniques for development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of epistolary form
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story is composed entirely of letters, diary entries, or these days even emails or blog posts, it is known as an epistolary style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes historically famous examples (Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe) and that authors have incorporated letters into novels since around the 15th century. Epistolary pieces can be entire works or partial—many famous authors use partial epistolary form to avoid structural difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of monologic / dialogic / polylogic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary novels can be monologic (focus on one character's letters/diary), dialogic (correspondence between two characters), or polylogic (multiple characters represented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the structure to match the story's aims: monologic (example: The Perks of Being a Wallflower) creates intimacy; polylogic (example: Les Liaisons dangereuses) uses alternating letters to foster uncertainty about who to trust and can create an air of gossip and mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct character voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow your protagonist and supporting cast to have their own distinct voices and individual ways of looking at the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistolary form is particularly useful for character development because each correspondent's writing reveals personality. Ensure each letter-writer sounds unique in diction, tone, and perspective to avoid flattening characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear distinction between writing style and viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a clear idea of how to distinguish between characters, both their writing styles and their viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately craft differences in syntax, vocabulary, formality, and outlook so readers can identify authorship and perspective without intrusive tags; mixing voice and viewpoint can confuse the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain dramatic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain your dramatic structure while using only letters—avoid losing plot momentum or coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article warns this is a major challenge of fully epistolary novels and is a common reason authors opt for partial epistolary techniques. Plan how plot beats are revealed across documents so narrative arc remains satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make chronology clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the chronology of your novel clear while using letters, which can otherwise obscure time relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because correspondence can be fragmented, provide dates, contextual cues, or reliable sequencing strategies to help readers follow temporal order; failure to do so is an anti-pattern that leads to confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epistolary form to evoke mood and reader response
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters/diary entries to evoke dramatic moods (sentiment, gossip, mystery) and to shape how readers judge trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternating letters can let readers wonder who to trust and create an air of gossip and mystery; choose the form to support intended emotional or thematic effects rather than as a gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic, firsthand narrator voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Write as if the person experiencing events is telling the story—nobody can tell a story better than the person it's happening to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor immediacy and specificity appropriate to a personal letter or diary entry; authenticity in how events and feelings are reported enhances believability and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and research correspondence forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice by reading historical letters or diary entries (or personal past writings) to learn how correspondence is structured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying real letters/diaries helps you replicate plausible rhythms, conventions, and structural cues. This is recommended as a concrete exercise to develop the technique and differentiate authentic-sounding voices.
